questions.explanation: The contribution of a state table is that it makes direction mean something. A stateless rule has to decide from the packet alone, and the usual way to let replies back in is to permit a whole direction of traffic, which is exactly the allowance an outbound connection wants. A stateful device records that the inside initiated a flow and keeps a table entry for it, so a returning packet is judged as part of that flow rather than as a fresh inbound connection claiming a destination port. That distinction is what removes the need for a blanket inbound allowance, and it is why a stateful rule set is usually much smaller and much more specific than a stateless one. The first distractor confuses payload inspection with flow tracking: content matching is a different feature, available in both kinds of device, and it is bounded by the fact that the content of an encrypted session is unreadable. The second confuses state with a lifetime, since a session timer is a separate feature that a stateful device may or may not have, and having one does nothing about how an unsolicited inbound packet is judged. The third is address translation, which is a separate function that happens to sit in the same box and has nothing to do with whether a flow was started by the inside. What a state table does not buy is any visibility into the content, and a flow established legitimately is still a channel an application will happily carry data out through.

questions.explanation: A state table answers one narrow question: has this flow already been admitted, and in which direction. Everything it says is a statement about a flow, and anything that is not a property of a flow is invisible to it. The first option is the clear case, because a machine inside the estate opening a connection to a destination on the internet produces packets that look like ordinary outbound traffic with a reply arriving on the same flow, and there is nothing about them that any state-based check can call wrong. The whole of the data leaving the building is carried on exactly the traffic the state check is designed to permit, which is why an exfiltration policy has to be written somewhere other than in the flow table. The second option is not a gap at all, because a state table records where a flow started, and it will see a packet claiming an inside source address on a flow it never saw begin, which is the case it exists to catch. The third is not true of a stateful design, and a device that discards its table on a reload is discarding the very thing that makes it stateful. The fourth describes the blind spot of flow tracking in general: the table says which flows exist and never what is inside them, so a permitted flow can be used for a purpose the rule never intended.

questions.explanation: The rule is justified by a statement about who needs to reach the server, and the statement is about a role rather than about a conversation. It assumes that everything arriving at that port is the continuation of a request some client outside legitimately made, and it has no way to hold that assumption to account. The consequence is that the rule converts a port into a standing invitation: once it is in place, anything that can open a connection to that port can do so, whether it is a client, a scanner, or a program that has found its way onto a machine and is now talking to the server directly. The check that closes this is not a longer list of permitted sources, which grows forever and is wrong on the first day a partner changes, but a check on the conversation itself: the inbound traffic must belong to a flow the server actually started, and a flow the server did not start is refused. That is a one-line change in a stateful device and a rewrite in a stateless one, which is most of the argument for having one. The first distractor describes the worst feature of the rule, since a static port is discoverable in a scan and is exactly what such a rule advertises. The second confuses the rule with the control, since restricting the source addresses to a partner's range makes the rule narrower without making it a conversation check. The third is the belief that makes this rule survive review, and it is wrong on the same point as the first: the server is reachable from wherever the route reaches.

questions.explanation: A five-tuple is a description of where a packet is going, not of what it is doing. Every field in it is an addressing field, chosen by whoever opened the flow, and none of them carries any statement about the application, the user, or the purpose. So a rule built from them can say that traffic from this address to that port on that protocol is acceptable, and it cannot say anything at all about whether the traffic on that flow is a query or an extraction, whether the client is the one it claims to be, or how much is on the flow. Two flows that match the same rule identically can be carrying entirely different things, and the rule will treat them the same. The consequences run in both directions. In the permissive direction, a flow admitted for a narrow purpose becomes a general channel and the application on the other end will usually not care what the request looks like. In the restrictive direction, an attempt to encode purpose into the rule by restricting ports produces rules that either break the application or get widened until they do not. The first distractor describes what a stateful device adds, which is a statement about a conversation rather than about an address, and it is a different feature from a five-tuple match. The second describes a separate kind of control, a filter at the name or layer that carries the content. The third assumes the rule set is being misapplied to traffic it was never written for, which is a real problem but not a property of the fields involved.

questions.explanation: The three properties that matter are the number of reachable pairs, the size of the group that is trusted together, and whether the policy can express the difference between two hosts in the same group. A zone collapses every host in it into one unit for the purposes of permission, so a server allowed to talk to one application server in its zone is allowed to talk to all of them, and an application server compromised in one place inherits every other application's reach in that zone. A per-host policy removes that collapse, so compromise of one host is bounded by that host's own entry rather than by the whole zone, and the thing being bounded is the number of pairs rather than the number of groups. The second gain is specificity: a policy written per host can record that host A needs to reach host B and not host C, which is expressible only if the policy unit is the host, and that is the difference between a policy someone can verify and a policy nobody can check. The third gain is that a per-host policy can be produced from what the host actually needs, since a host's own traffic is a short list, whereas a zone policy has to be inferred from a guess about the group's role. What it does not buy is any reduction in the number of rules to maintain, and that is the honest cost: the design replaces a small fuzzy policy with a large precise one, and it only works if the precise one is generated rather than written by hand.
questions.hint: Ask what two hosts inside the same zone are assumed to share.

questions.explanation: A virtual LAN is a label attached to a switch port, and the switch consults that label when it decides where to forward a frame. Two things follow. The first is that the separation is a forwarding decision, not a channel: a broadcast frame still reaches every port in the same virtual LAN, and a host that is a member of both can carry traffic between them, which is a supported configuration and a common source of unintended reach. The second is that the label is a claim about which port something is plugged into, and a device that can talk to the switch can ask to be put on a different one, or can be put there by someone who can. So the boundary is real for a correctly configured, non-participating estate and it is a convention once anything on the segment can speak to the switch. What it does not do is separate the two groups from each other at any layer below, so members of one virtual LAN can still affect a host in the other through shared infrastructure such as a name service, a management interface, or a power and cooling path. The first distractor names a genuine gap, which is that a host deliberately joined to both groups defeats the boundary, but the arrangement is routinely treated as if it were a single boundary and that is the error. The second is about hosts rather than about the configuration, and a host that ignores the boundary is a host problem. The third is a timing question with a real answer and nothing to do with what is being isolated.
questions.hint: Ask what the label is a claim about, and who else can speak to the device that enforces it.

questions.explanation: On an ordinary access switch every port reaches every other port on the same switch through the same physical wire, and the only thing keeping one user's machine off another's is that the switch treats each port as a separate domain. That works, and it is a lot of hardware for what it does, and it fails in one specific way: any device that can speak the addressing protocol can ask the switch to deliver frames to a port it is not plugged into. A private virtual LAN takes the delivery decision away from that device by making the switch refuse to forward between member ports at all, so the host on the port can talk to the gateway and to nothing else in the group, and the ability to request a delivery is simply not one of the things it has. The class of mistake this prevents is a host, or anything impersonating one on that wire, choosing for itself which other port it talks to. It does not affect what the host can reach through the gateway, and it is emphatically not a control on traffic leaving the switch, because the switch still forwards the host's traffic to the wider network exactly as before. The first distractor describes what the arrangement prevents and is the right answer at the wrong level of generality, since the useful statement is about who chooses the destination. The second confuses the arrangement with a switch-wide policy, which is a different feature and applies to every port rather than to this one.

What it does not buy is identity. questions.explanation: Address translation rewrites the source or destination field in the header of each packet, and it does that and nothing else. What survives untouched is everything the field did not carry: the number of internal hosts talking, which they talk to, how much, how often, and for how long. It also leaves the boundary in plain view, because a single outside address with a large number of distinct internal conversations behind it is a signal in itself, and one inside host that suddenly talks to a new set of destinations is visible without any address being named. So the arrangement is a real reduction in what an outside observer can say about the internal naming and numbering, and it is routinely described in exactly those terms, which is where the misbelief comes from. It is not a control on reach, because it does not refuse anything: every internal host remains able to reach every destination it could reach before, and a compromise of one of them is not bounded by it. The first distractor is the one that makes it worth doing, and describing it as concealment is accurate. The second is the ordinary confusion, treating a change in addressing as though it were a change in permission. The third attributes to it a filtering function, which is a separate feature that has to be configured separately and is the one that actually bounds reach.

questions.explanation: Origin validation answers a narrow question: did an announcement for this prefix come from a provider authorised to speak for the prefix's owner? That is worth having and it does remove a large class of misconfiguration, but a legitimate provider is a network, not an identity, and a network can be induced to accept and originate an announcement it was never asked to originate. So a correctly signed, correctly originated announcement can still point at an address range that the real owner did not intend to be reachable through that provider, and origin validation has nothing to say about it because the chain of authority it checks is intact. What closes the gap is a second, different fact: the prefix was registered to that provider in the first place. Registered origin data is published for exactly this purpose, and a validator that checks an announcement against it can tell the difference between a provider speaking for a prefix it holds and a provider repeating a prefix that someone else holds. questions.explanation: The record is a claim published in the domain's own name zone, listing the addresses that may send on its behalf, and the party that consults it is the receiving mail server, not the sending one and not the user. The field it is compared against is the address in the message's envelope, the one that names the server which was asked to deliver it, and not the name displayed in the message as its sender. That distinction is the whole design and it is where the failure mode lives: because the envelope address is set by the sending system and the visible name is set by whoever composed the message, a message can pass this check and still display a completely different sender to the reader, and a great many legitimate messages do exactly that. The check is also only a statement about hosts, since the list is a set of servers and says nothing about which account on an allowed server sent the message, so a compromised account on an authorised host is a successful sender as far as this check is concerned. And the pass is not an authentication of the content: it means the envelope sender was permitted, and nothing about who read it or why. The first distractor is the opposite misreading, treating the record as covering the visible sender, which is precisely what it does not do.

questions.explanation: The signature covers a chosen set of header fields and the body, and the set is chosen at signing time and then declared in the signature itself, so a verifier knows what was covered rather than having to guess. The fields that are normally left outside are the ones added by the infrastructure the message crosses on the way: the trace headers that each mail server appends as it handles the message, and often the visible sender field as well. That exclusion is deliberate rather than an oversight, and it is what allows a message to travel at all. If the visible sender were signed, then the one legitimate case that cannot be signed is the one where a message is forwarded, because forwarding rewrites that field and the signature would be broken by a step the sender had no part in. So the design trades coverage of the visible sender for reachability of forwarded mail, and puts the burden on a second mechanism to handle the field it had to leave open. The consequence a defender has to hold is that a valid signature proves the signed headers and the body are unmodified and were produced by a key holder, and says nothing by itself about the name the message displays. The first distractor reverses the direction of the omission and blames the verifying side. The second claims the signature covers the displayed name, which is exactly the coverage that was given up.

questions.explanation: A signature is a claim by a key holder about a set of signed headers, and the whole of what it establishes is that the holder produced this content and nobody has modified it since. What it does not establish is a relationship between the key holder and the name a reader sees, because a signature can be perfectly valid and the message can still display a sender belonging to somebody else. Requiring the match is what supplies that missing relationship: the authenticated domain and the displayed domain have to be the same, and a message where they are not is a message where a valid signature is being used as a borrowed credential for a name it has nothing to do with. That is the specific thing this mechanism closes, and it is why publishing it changes the economics of the attack rather than its rate: before it, any key holder could sign mail that displayed anyone; after it, only a key holder for the displayed domain can produce a message that authenticates for that domain. The distinction it cannot make is between a message the domain's own people sent and a message sent by an account inside that domain, since both authenticate identically. The first distractor claims the rule is about the body's content. The second claims it is about the visible sender's format, which is a different check entirely.

questions.explanation: The escrow copy is what converts encryption from a control into a policy, and both halves of that are worth stating. questions.explanation: The measurements are a running record, extended at each stage, of the identity of every component that has executed so far. Because each stage checks the record left by the one before, and because the record is held in hardware the software itself cannot rewrite, the chain establishes a statement about the history of the boot: these specific components, in this order, produced this final state. That is what makes a remote party willing to release a secret to the machine, since the secret is bound to the measurements rather than released to anything that merely claims to be the machine. What it establishes is a statement about the start-up path, and that is the limit of it. The chain is measured up to the point where a full operating system takes over, and once a general-purpose system is running, the record says nothing about what that system does next: a program loaded afterwards, a module inserted, a device given a page, none of it is covered by what the boot stages recorded. So the property is that the machine booted correctly, not that the machine is behaving correctly, and the two are routinely quoted as though they were the same claim. The first distractor extends the chain into the running system, which is the common overstatement. The second confuses the record with a signature, and it is important to be clear that the record is a measurement, not a proof: it is evidence a remote party weighs, not something that cannot be produced.

questions.explanation: The value sits between the function's own data and the point the function will resume at, and a corruption that reaches downwards from the local variables to the return address has to pass through the position the value occupies. So on return, a value that has changed means something overwrote the frame, and the function refuses to return to a corrupted address. That is a detection, and the distinction from prevention matters: the overwrite has already happened, the check is what notices, and the only thing the check does is refuse to continue. Its coverage is exactly the frame it was placed in. It does nothing for data elsewhere in the process: a heap object, a global, another function's frame on a different thread, and an overwrite that changes values without reaching a return address are all untouched by it, and many of them are as damaging. Nor does it help if the value itself is disclosed, because a party who knows the value can overwrite it with the same value and the check will pass. The reason the mechanism is still worth having is that it converts the easiest and most common way of taking over a process into a crash, which is loud, and that is a meaningful reduction even though it is not a repair. If the pages holding data cannot be executed, then a corrupted pointer aimed at those pages cannot be made to run, whatever is in them, and the data has to be made to look like code before it can be of any use. What it does not stop is code reuse. An attacker who can corrupt a pointer does not have to supply any code at all: there is already code in the process that performs the operation they want, and pointing a return address at the right existing instruction performs it. So the arrangement removes the technique that requires injected code and leaves the technique that requires none, and the honest summary is that it raises the cost of a class of attack rather than removing a class of attacker. questions.explanation: The two features are halves of one mechanism, and the reason is that each supplies something the other cannot learn on its own. The snooping feature watches address-assignment traffic arriving on untrusted ports and records which address was offered to which port, and that is the only way a switch can find out which machine is on which socket, because a machine never says which port it is behind. The inspection feature then watches address-resolution traffic and insists that a claim about which address lives on which port matches a snooped binding, and that is the only way a switch can stop a machine on one socket claiming to be a machine on another. questions.explanation: The weakness is that the check answers a different question from the one the device needs answered. Holding four keys and accepting any of them establishes that the image came from somebody the vendor trusts, and there is no way from the image alone to say which of the four was supposed to sign it. That matters because the four keys do not have the same reach even when the vendor is the holder of all of them. A key that signs a general release and a key that signs a debug, test or factory image are different authorities even inside one organisation, and a device that accepts both cannot enforce the separation between them, so a fault or a compromise of the narrow one is immediately a fault of the broad one. It also means revocation becomes impossible: a key that has to be withdrawn cannot be, because withdrawing it removes the ability to accept the images it was supposed to sign as well, and the device has no way to accept some releases and reject others while both are signed by keys it holds. questions.explanation: The cap is a blunt instrument and it is worth being blunt about why it is still useful. It catches the pattern that is hardest to see: a host that has been compromised quietly and is moving data out over weeks in a volume that no single transfer flags and that an ordinary volume report would not have been read to notice. The alarm is the part that matters, because the cap alone is a limit and a limit nobody watches is not a control. What it misses is everything below the line. A transfer of a few hundred megabytes a month is well inside any cap worth setting, and a database, a source repository, a photo library, or a compressed archive of something small can each be worth more than a cap-sized volume, so a targeted collection leaves by a route the cap does not question. It also says nothing about a transfer to a destination that is already trusted, which is where a great deal of real loss goes, and nothing about data that never leaves in bulk because it leaves in a message body. The honest framing is that this is a tripwire for the large and the sustained rather than a limit on the capability. The first distractor turns the cap into a complete control on the host's reach. The second confuses the cap with a rate limit on a connection, which is a different mechanism. The third reverses the alarm's purpose.

questions.explanation: The change removes one technique outright and leaves the rest of the class intact, and the distinction is the whole of its value. An attacker who has corrupted a pointer no longer needs to write their own instructions somewhere and point at them, because the pages an injection would need cannot be executed; that is a technique gone, not a technique made harder. What remains is code reuse, which requires no injected code at all, since the instruction sequence the attacker wants is already in the process and pointing at it is enough. For that, the address of existing code is the obstacle, and a separate measure deals with it by making the layout unpredictable, so the two belong together and neither substitutes for the other. The second thing the change does not remove is the corruption itself. Nothing about non-executable memory stops a pointer being overwritten, a structure being forged, or a check being bypassed by a value the program is willing to accept, and those are the majority of what a program-security defect actually consists of. So the honest report says the cost of one route rose and the defect is still there, which is a different sentence from the one that says the class was closed. The first distractor claims the change removes the whole class. The second claims it makes reuse harder, which is the work of a different measure. questions.explanation: Replacing a key buys the one thing that short validity and encryption alone cannot: it removes the standing value of a copy that was taken. If a machine's key was read at some point in the past, a new key means the copy in the other party's hands opens nothing, and the exposure ends for that machine at the moment the change happens rather than whenever the disk happens to be replaced. That is a real and specific benefit and it is the reason rotation on hardware belongs on the schedule rather than in the exceptions list. The thing the plan has to be careful about is ordering, and there is exactly one safe order. The new key has to be established and confirmed before the old one is destroyed, and a machine in between the two states is a machine whose data is protected by nothing at all, which is worse than a machine that never moved. A plan that runs at scale therefore needs a way to tell which machines are in that window, and a way to hold the old key for a machine that has not yet been confirmed, and both of those are operational properties rather than technical ones. The first distractor claims rotation is what makes the encryption strong, which confuses a property of the key with a property of the mechanism. The second claims the risk is that the new key leaks, when the risk in the plan is the interval with neither.

questions.explanation: The order is set by one dependency and one practical constraint. The measurement has to exist before it can be sent, so the device has to be recording before anything is transmitted, and a service that is receiving values for machines that are not yet enrolled is a service that cannot tell a new machine from a changed one. The constraint is that the recording has to survive the changes the enrolment itself makes, which is why provisioning sits before sealing: adding the device to the estate, giving it a key the service recognises, and letting it record a state that the service has a reference for are all things that change the measured values, and a reference captured before them will never match. questions.explanation: B is the one that matters most, and the reason is not the absence of encryption. It is that staff devices and devices belonging to visitors are on one network, which means anything a visitor brings is a member of the same broadcast domain as every staff machine, can see their traffic, and can be talked to as though it were local. The encryption setting is the lesser half of the problem; the shared membership is the larger one, and it is the half that an open network's protection setting does not address at all. A is the weakest of the three that authenticate, because one secret held by 300 people means every one of them holds the key that protects every other one's traffic and a recorded association is enough to test that one secret offline, and it also means the secret leaves whenever any of the 300 leaves. C is the arrangement to work towards: the credential is per device, revocation is individual, and a captured association reveals nothing about any other device. D is C with one important addition, since the pre-authentication network is where a device sits until it has a credential, and the reason it matters is that without it a device that has not authenticated has nowhere to be except alongside the ones that have. So the ranking is B, then A, then D as a refinement of C, and C as the target.

questions.explanation: D is the weakest and the reason is worth spelling out because the configuration looks like the strongest one on paper. The disk is encrypted and the key is released only for the expected start-up, so the design has done everything right locally. And then the recovery copy, which is the key to all of it, is written to the same disk under the same encryption, which means it is protected by exactly the mechanism it exists to recover from. It is a single point of failure that fails at the moment it is needed, and it also means the property the encryption was bought for is now held in a file whose loss loses both the data and the way to read it. A is the strongest of the four, because it does the two local things correctly and puts the recovery copy somewhere with different exposure and, implicitly, somewhere with a different set of controls. C is not encrypted at all, which is a serious finding, but it fails in an obvious way that an assessment will find and a device in a lost-property store will not. B is encrypted with the key in the user's own hands, so a machine in a lost-property store is protected and a user who loses their own key has lost the data, which is the trade escrow exists to remove. The ranking is D, C, B, A.

questions.explanation: A supports the strongest claim, and the reason is the reference rather than the recording. Recording a measurement is cheap and only produces a statement about what ran; holding a value the measurement is checked against turns that statement into something a remote party can rely on, because the check is what fails when the path changes. A has both halves, and it therefore supports the claim that this machine started the way the estate expects. B has only the first half, so it establishes that the firmware accepted signed components and nothing about whether the record of that start-up could be compared against anything. D is the interesting one, because it records more than B and yet supports a weaker claim: a log of measurements nobody checks is an observation with no comparison, and a party reading it after the fact learns what happened rather than obtaining assurance that it happened as expected, and a measurement in a local log can be edited by anything that runs on the machine. C is the weakest, since it has neither the check nor the record, and the documented setting means the check can be removed by anyone who can boot the machine. So the ordering is A, then B, then D, then C.

answer.exemplar: The limit is where a design decision meets an adversary, and that is why it belongs in a security review rather than only in a capacity plan. A flow table exists so that a returning packet can be recognised as part of a conversation the inside began, rather than as a fresh inbound connection asking for a service. Every entry is therefore load-bearing: it is what a policy decision is recorded in, and a table without room to record a new flow has no way to take a decision about it. The device deals with the shortage in one of two ways, and they have opposite security consequences. If it drops the newest flow, then a party that has deliberately filled the table gets to choose which traffic is never examined, and every host behind the device that was not already in the table is unprotected until the entries expire. If it drops the oldest, the party instead gets to evict the estate's real conversations and force the honest ones to be re-established and re-decided. Either way the property that is lost is not bandwidth, it is the guarantee that traffic was judged, and the symptom is silence rather than an error, which is why an exhausted table is so often mistaken for a quiet period. That is what makes the limit a security parameter. It has to be sized well above the honest peak concurrency, since an undersized table is an availability incident and an oversized one is a target, and the ratio between the two is the design's real constraint. It has to be alarmed on before it is reached, and the alarm has to be interpreted correctly: a rising count is a capacity signal and a sudden plateau on every estate host at once is a different signal entirely. And an idle timeout on entries is not optional housekeeping, because a table whose entries never expire is a table that can be filled and then held indefinitely. The most useful artefact an estate can have here is not the limit itself but a rehearsed answer to the question of what the device is doing while the table is full, because on most devices the honest answer is that it is forwarding.

questions.explanation: The table is finite and the traffic is not. Each admitted flow costs an entry, and the entries are what make a returning packet recognisable as part of a conversation. Once the table is full, new flows are dropped without a decision, so the whole policy stops applying to whatever was trying to open them, and an attacker can fill the table on purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the policy when the table is full and new flows are dropped.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a flow table limit is a security parameter rather than a capacity setting

answer.exemplar: The problem is the shape rather than the year, and the shape is wrong in three separate ways that all follow from one decision. A single passphrase is expanded into a single key that every client then uses, so the network has no notion of one user being unable to read another user. Confidentiality between two colleagues on the same wireless network is not a property the network provides at all; it is a property of the colleagues not reading each other's traffic. That is a social control, and social controls do not scale with headcount, they degrade with it, because each additional holder both widens the set of people who can read every session and adds another copy that has to be kept. The second consequence is that revocation has become a site-wide operation. The secret is the unit of authorisation, so withdrawing one person's access means rotating the secret for everybody, and the rotation is only complete when every holder has actually changed it, which is a distributed operation with no completion signal and a long tail of devices that nobody got to. A compromise of the secret is the same event at a larger scale: there is one thing to steal, it is worth everything on the network, and finding out who took it is not possible because there is one credential and no record of who used it. The third consequence is the one that makes the passphrase itself the weak point rather than merely the architecture. The authentication exchange has to convince the other end that it holds the secret, and the way it does that involves a value computed from the derived key, which means a single recorded exchange is a permanent offline test against a guessed passphrase, repeatable as often as the attacker likes with no further contact. So the entire network's confidentiality ends up resting on the entropy of a string a person chose and will be tempted to write on a sticker. The replacement does not improve the parameter, it changes the shape. Give each device its own credential so that no holder holds another device's key and removal is individual, and derive the session key from values exchanged for that session and not reusable afterwards so that a recording yields nothing to test a guess against. The same argument applies to any shared secret in a system that has to grow, and the question worth asking in a design review is not how well the secret was chosen but what one copy of it is worth.

questions.explanation: One secret produces one key, so every holder can read every other session, and the secret is also the unit of revocation, which makes every removal a site-wide change. Scale multiplies both properties rather than diluting them.
questions.hint: Ask what a single copy of the secret is worth, and what happens to it when one person leaves.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a shared-secret design fails to scale independently of its age

answer.exemplar: Encryption on a laptop answers one question, which is whether a disk in somebody else's hands yields anything. Both designs answer it, and the difference between them is not a matter of degree. The first design keeps the unlocking key inside the platform's secure hardware and releases it only when the recorded start-up state matches what was expected, so the guarantee the estate can make is a statement about the machine: if the disk is removed it does not read, and if the start-up path is changed it does not read. That is a property of the estate's estate, and it can be stated to somebody outside it. It also has a cost that has to be paid deliberately rather than discovered: there is now a single store that can unlock every laptop, which makes that store the most valuable secret the organisation holds and makes access to it the most attractive thing to instrument. A programme that adopts the first design and does not treat the recovery store accordingly has converted a distributed problem into a concentrated one and then managed it as though nothing changed. The second design releases the key to the person who signs in, which is a reasonable choice for a machine that leaves the building and a very different one for a fleet. The estate can no longer make a statement about the machine; it can make a statement about every user who has ever been trusted with their own key, and that statement degrades in exactly the ways people degrade, since credentials get written down, asked for by a convincing stranger, shared with a colleague who needs the file, and forgotten. There is also no recovery path, so the day a user loses the key the data is gone, and the predictable result is a request for a bypass, which is a far worse outcome than the one the design was adopted to avoid. Neither design is wrong by default and the choice is genuinely a trade, but the difference between them is the programme rather than a detail inside it, and it is worth noticing that most of the checklist items in this area are identical in both designs while the two outcomes are not comparable.

questions.explanation: It decides what the estate's property depends on. With the key in the platform, the guarantee is a statement about the machine and there is one choke point; with the key in the user's hands, the guarantee becomes a statement about every person trusted with their own key.
questions.hint: Ask where the key has to come from in each design, and what the estate can state about its machines.

answer.exemplar: The confusion is between two properties, and it persists because the two are genuinely correlated. What the mechanism does is rewrite an address in a header as traffic passes through, and from that single fact it produces a real result: the internal numbering scheme is not published on the wire, so a party who has not been inside the estate cannot say which range is in use or name a host in it. That is worth having, it is a real reduction in what an observer can infer, and describing it as concealment is accurate. What everybody assumes it also does is bound reach, and it does not, because the mechanism never refuses anything. Every internal host can still reach every destination it could reach before it was installed, a compromised host is exactly as compromised as it was, and anything able to address the translated address is still able to reach whatever is behind it. The gap is not subtle in principle; it is subtle in practice because the two properties travel together in every demonstration anyone has seen. Someone shows that the internal address cannot be seen, and the room concludes that the internal host cannot be reached, and the second conclusion is the one that changes the design. The consequence is a specific failure in the review process rather than merely an inaccuracy in a document. Translation appears in the control list, so the question of what bounds the estate's internal reach has been answered, and the filtering rules that would answer it are never written, or are written narrowly and quietly not enforced. The second-order effect is that the translation device becomes a single point through which all outbound traffic passes, with none of the monitoring, the capability restriction, or the inspection that would otherwise be expected of the estate's main boundary, because nobody thinks of it as a boundary. The useful way to handle it in a design review is to write down the two sentences separately: the mechanism reduces what can be inferred about internal naming, and reach is bounded by the filtering policy and by nothing else. And the pattern generalises, which is why it is worth recognising rather than merely fixing here. A mechanism that changes an identifier, a label, a name, or an address gets credited with the property of the thing the identifier was pointing at, and the review then stops looking for the control that was never installed.

questions.hint: Ask whether the mechanism can refuse a packet, and what it does to the name in the header.

questions.explanation: There are ten choices for each of the four positions and the choices are independent, so the space is ten to the fourth, which is 10000, and the fact that repeats are allowed is what keeps it at that rather than falling by a factor of ten for each position. The number matters because it is the size of the space an attacker has to search and it is small enough that the search is a matter of arithmetic rather than of endurance, which is why the controls around a short code are about rate and about what the code alone can reach rather than about the code being unguessable. At a hundred attempts a second the whole space is exhausted in a hundred seconds, and at a thousand a second in ten, so any device that permits an unlimited number of attempts has a code of four digits as its weakest link by a wide margin. What actually makes a short code acceptable is everything around it: a limit on attempts followed by a lockout, a delay, or an erasure; a requirement that the device attest to its own integrity before it accepts an attempt; and a rule about how much the code alone can reach. Those are the controls, and the number above is the argument for having them.

questions.explanation: Three thousand hosts at five gigabytes each is fifteen thousand gigabytes, and the reason the arithmetic is worth doing is that the figure is not an abstraction when somebody has to provision it. Fifteen thousand gigabytes is the capacity the network has to carry if every host is genuinely using its allowance, which is fifteen terabytes and is a real number to design a link and a metering plan around, and it is the figure a capacity argument in a design review will be settled with. The more instructive direction is the other one. A cap set high enough not to disturb honest use across three thousand hosts has to accommodate whatever the estate's normal aggregate is, so the alert threshold derived from it will sit far above the volume a deliberate collection produces, and the cap therefore functions as a tripwire for the large and the sustained rather than as a limit on the capability. It also does nothing about a host that is compromised and reads a store that is already inside, since the transfer is measured against a denominator that includes the whole estate. So the cap is worth having, and the figure it produces is the reason it is not the control people assume it is.
